The continuum-local-setup repo gives you a single docker compose up that launches the complete Project Continuum stack — infrastructure services, platform backend, browser IDE, and feature workers — all wired together and ready to go.

Project Continuum is an open-source, browser-native visual workflow platform — inspired by KNIME, built for the cloud. You design workflows as a drag-and-drop graph of nodes, and the platform runs them durably: a crashed worker, a dead Kafka broker, or a dropped connection doesn't lose your progress.

All data passed between workflow nodes is Apache Parquet (Snappy-compressed, Avro schema DataRow) — not JSON. This keeps data columnar, compressed, and query-ready from the moment it leaves a node. Apache ParquetSnappyAvro schema DataRow ✍️Writing NodeOutputWriter.OutputPortWriter writes rows to the node's output port(s). 📖Reading NodeInputReader reads rows from each connected input port. 🏷️File names Output files are named output.{portId}.parquet; input files input.{portId}.parquet. 🗂️Staging Files are staged in a local cache path before upload to (or after download from) MinIO, the platform's S3-compatible object store. Mix and match workers Because every node reads and writes the same Parquet/Avro format regardless of which worker or language implements it, nodes written in different feature repos — base analytics, cheminformatics, AI/ML — can be freely wired together in the same workflow graph.

Every workflow node is defined inside a feature worker — an independent service (e.g. continuum-feature-base, continuum-feature-ai, continuum-feature-cheminformatics, or your own) built with the continuum-worker-springboot-starter. Workers register their nodes centrally so the orchestration service knows which worker to dispatch each node to.

Every node: Is annotated @ContinuumNode (not just @Component) — enforced at build time by a Gradle validation task and at startup by the node activity handler. Extends ProcessNodeModel (data nodes) or TriggerNodeModel (source nodes). Overrides inputPorts, outputPorts, and metadata (as ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodeData). Implements execute() — the simple overload for most nodes, or the ExecutionContext overload for nodes that need credentials. MyNodeModel.kt @ContinuumNode class MyNodeModel : ProcessNodeModel() { override val inputPorts = mapOf("input" to ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort(...)) override val outputPorts = mapOf("output" to ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort(...)) override val metadata = ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodeData(...) override fun execute( properties: Map<String, Any>?, inputs: Map<String, NodeInputReader>, nodeOutputWriter: NodeOutputWriter, nodeProgressCallback: NodeProgressCallback, executionContext: ExecutionContext // only needed for credential access ) { /* ... */ } } Node documentation is auto-loaded from resources/<package>/<ClassName>.doc.md on startup.

At startup, each worker publishes its available nodes to Kafka so the platform can build a central registry of "which node lives on which worker": On ApplicationReadyEvent, the worker iterates every ContinuumNodeModel bean it has. For each node, it builds a FeatureRegistrationRequest — containing nodeId (fully-qualified class name), workerId, featureId, taskQueue, a JSON nodeManifest (ports, schemas, title, icon), and the node's documentation markdown — and publishes it to Kafka (Avro, keyed by nodeId). continuum-message-bridge consumes the message and performs an atomic upsert into the registered_nodes table. The orchestration service's InitializeActivity later queries this registry (via the API server) to resolve which task queue should run each node in a workflow. featureId is derived by stripping the trailing .node package segment from the class name, e.g. org.projectcontinuum.feature.analytics.node.CreateTableNodeModel → org.projectcontinuum.feature.analytics. nodeManifest is kept as an opaque JSON string (not typed Avro fields) so the schema stays forward-compatible as NodeData evolves. Registration is one message per node, enabling clean idempotent upserts, and extensions (a map<string>) is reserved for future fields without breaking schema compatibility.

documents.t: Nodes that need external secrets (API keys, DB passwords) don't receive them automatically: The node's propertiesUISchema declares a control with options.format = "credential" purely so continuum-workbench renders a credential picker in its config dialog — the backend doesn't read this schema. Inside execute(), the node reads its own properties to find the configured credential name, then calls executionContext.getCredential<T>(name). This fetches the credential on demand from continuum-credentials-server (GET /api/v1/credentials/{name}) and deserializes it into T, throwing if not found. Credentials are never stored in the workflow Credentials are fetched lazily, per execution — never bundled into the workflow definition or passed through Kafka.
Continuum is split into a browser frontend, a core backend (API server + Temporal orchestration), and independent feature workers that provide the actual workflow nodes.

You design a workflow in the browser (React Flow canvas) and hit Execute. continuum-api-server receives the REST call and starts a Temporal workflow (ContinuumWorkflow, on WORKFLOW_TASK_QUEUE). InitializeActivity resolves which task queue (= which worker) handles each node, via POST /api/v1/node-explorer/nodes/task-queues against the API server's node registry. For each DAG node, IContinuumNodeActivity.run() is dispatched to the resolved worker's task queue (ACTIVITY_TASK_QUEUE). The worker downloads input Parquet from MinIO, runs execute(), and uploads output Parquet. Nodes run in parallel where the DAG allows — ContinuumWorkflow waits for the first pending node to complete, then schedules newly unblocked nodes. Each node sends progress signals; ContinuumWorkflow publishes a WorkflowUpdateEvent to Kafka. continuum-message-bridge consumes the Kafka event and republishes it to Mosquitto (MQTT). The browser receives the update over MQTT-over-WebSocket and lights up the corresponding node in real time. The same flow as a sequence:

Crash-proof by design Temporal persists workflow state (in PostgreSQL) at every step. If a worker process dies mid-execution, the orchestration service simply redispatches the pending activity once a worker becomes available again — no data loss, no restart from scratch. This is the "crash-proof execution" promise: a failed Kafka broker, a restarted worker pod, or a dropped network connection doesn't lose workflow progress.

Three Temporal task queues coordinate the system: Queue Consumer Purpose WORKFLOW_TASK_QUEUE ContinuumWorkflow (orchestration service) Drives the DAG execution loop ACTIVITY_TASK_QUEUE ContinuumNodeActivity (feature workers) Runs individual node logic — name overridable per worker via continuum.core.worker.node-task-queue ACTIVITY_TASK_QUEUE_INITIALIZE InitializeActivity (orchestration service) Resolves node → task queue routing before dispatch See Node Model & Registration for how a worker's nodes end up in that registry in the first place, and Data Format for how data actually moves between nodes.

Continuum is designed to be extended by adding new workers, not modifying existing ones — see Node Model & Feature Registration for why that's safe to do independently. To build your own set of nodes, start from continuum-feature-template — a scaffold for a standalone Gradle project with the Spring Boot worker setup, Temporal registration, and @ContinuumNode conventions already wired up. tip The template builds against platform 0.0.20 out of the box and includes a Kotlin and a Java example node, CI/CD workflows, a Helm chart and a local Docker stack. For a step-by-step walkthrough of cloning it, renaming it, writing your first node (in Kotlin or Java) and shipping it, see Create New Nodes. Once your worker is running and registering nodes, it can be deployed as an independent release into the same Kubernetes namespace as the core platform (see Deployment) — no changes to continuum-platform-core or any other feature repo required. For questions or to report issues, use the GitHub issue tracker on the core repo.

Start from the continuum-feature-template repository, rename it, replace its example node with yours, and ship a worker. You write one Kotlin or Java class per node. The template provides everything else. Kotlin or Java6 stepsPlatform 0.0.20

A node is a block on the Workbench canvas that reads tables, does something and writes tables. Nodes live in a feature worker, a small Spring Boot app that registers its nodes with the platform at startup. You don't build a worker from scratch. The template is already a complete, working worker with two example nodes (one Kotlin, one Java), a build, tests, CI/CD, a Helm chart and a local stack. Your job is to rename it and swap in your own nodes.

Requirement Notes JDK 21 Eclipse Temurin recommended. Check with java -version. Docker and Compose Runs the local Continuum stack, about 8 GB of RAM. Some Kotlin or Java You don't need to know Temporal, Kafka or Spring internals. A GitHub account The template is used from GitHub, and the release steps run on GitHub Actions. You don't need a GitHub token, and you don't need to install Gradle: the repository includes the wrapper. Everything comes from Maven Central. To publish your work you also need Docker Hub (or another registry) credentials, and optionally a Maven Central account; Step 6 covers both.

documents.t: After Step 5Kotlin examples Step 4 builds one process node. This page covers what you reach for next. The Kotlin code on this page was compiled and its tests were run against platform 0.0.20. Java versions follow the same shape as the Java Word Counter in Step 4, and the notes below say where the API differs.

You don't need a new module for every node. Add another class to the same package: Create <package>/node/MyOtherNodeModel.kt next to your first node, annotated with @ContinuumNode. Add MyOtherNodeModel.doc.md in the matching resources folder. Add a test. Bump featureVersion and the chart's appVersion before you ship (Step 6). That's all. AutoConfigure already scans your whole package, so there is nothing to register. Rebuild and restart the worker; it logs every node it found: Registered process nodes: [com.acme.demo.node.WordCounterNodeModel, com.acme.demo.node.MyOtherNodeModel] Registered trigger nodes: [...] Create a second module only when you want to publish some nodes as a separate library, or keep unrelated nodes apart. A new module needs a folder under features/, an include(...) in settings.gradle.kts, an implementation(project(...)) in worker/build.gradle.kts, its own AutoConfigure and .imports file, and entries in the two workflow files. Step 2 lists everything that must agree.

A node that creates data from nothing (a generator, a file reader, an API poll) extends TriggerNodeModel instead of ProcessNodeModel. It has no inputPorts, and execute() has no inputs parameter: package com.acme.demo.node import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.annotation.ContinuumNode import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.model.ContinuumWorkflowModel import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.node.TriggerNodeModel import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.utils.NodeOutputWriter import org.springframework.http.MediaType.APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE @ContinuumNode class NumberGeneratorNodeModel : TriggerNodeModel() { final override val outputPorts = mapOf( "output" to ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort(name = "Numbers", contentType = APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE) ) override val categories = listOf("Demo") override val metadata = ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodeData( id = this.javaClass.name, nodeModel = this.javaClass.name, title = "Number Generator", subTitle = "Create a table of numbers", description = "Creates a table with a number column and its square", outputs = outputPorts, properties = mapOf("count" to 10), propertiesSchema = mapOf( "type" to "object", "properties" to mapOf("count" to mapOf("type" to "integer", "title" to "Row Count", "minimum" to 1)), "required" to listOf("count") ), propertiesUISchema = mapOf( "type" to "VerticalLayout", "elements" to listOf(mapOf("type" to "Control", "scope" to "#/properties/count")) ) ) override fun execute(properties: Map<String, Any>?, nodeOutputWriter: NodeOutputWriter) { val count = (properties?.get("count") as Number?)?.toInt() ?: 10 nodeOutputWriter.createOutputPortWriter("output").use { writer -> for (n in 0 until count) { writer.write(n.toLong(), mapOf("n" to n, "square" to n * n)) } } } } Everything else from Step 4 applies: the .doc.md help page, the package rule, the row types and the test approach. In a test you call execute(properties, outputWriter) with just two arguments. This example builds its schemas with mapOf(...) instead of parsing JSON strings. Both styles work; mapOf needs no ObjectMapper.

documents.t: Nodes that call an API, a database or a cloud service shouldn't take secrets as plain settings. Store the secret as a credential in the platform, let the user pick it in the node's form, and read it in execute(). There are three pieces: The settings hold only the credential's name. The UI schema marks that control with options.format = "credential", so the Workbench shows a credential picker. execute() takes an extra ExecutionContext parameter and calls getCredential. package com.acme.demo.node import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.annotation.ContinuumNode import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.context.ExecutionContext import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.exception.NodeRuntimeException import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.model.ContinuumWorkflowModel import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.node.ProcessNodeModel import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.protocol.progress.NodeProgressCallback import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.utils.NodeInputReader import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.utils.NodeOutputWriter import org.springframework.http.MediaType.APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE @ContinuumNode class ApiLookupNodeModel : ProcessNodeModel() { final override val inputPorts = mapOf( "input" to ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort(name = "Input Table", contentType = APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE) ) final override val outputPorts = mapOf( "output" to ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort(name = "Output Table", contentType = APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE) ) override val categories = listOf("Demo") override val metadata = ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodeData( id = this.javaClass.name, nodeModel = this.javaClass.name, title = "API Lookup", description = "Calls an API with a stored credential", inputs = inputPorts, outputs = outputPorts, properties = mapOf("credential" to ""), propertiesSchema = mapOf( "type" to "object", "properties" to mapOf("credential" to mapOf("type" to "string", "title" to "Credential")), "required" to listOf("credential") ), propertiesUISchema = mapOf( "type" to "VerticalLayout", "elements" to listOf( mapOf( "type" to "Control", "scope" to "#/properties/credential", "options" to mapOf("format" to "credential", "credentialType" to "GENERIC") ) ) ) ) // The shape of the credential's key-value data data class ApiKey(val key: String) override fun execute( properties: Map<String, Any>?, inputs: Map<String, NodeInputReader>, nodeOutputWriter: NodeOutputWriter, nodeProgressCallback: NodeProgressCallback, executionContext: ExecutionContext ) { val name = properties?.get("credential") as String? ?: throw NodeRuntimeException(isRetriable = false, workflowId = "", nodeId = "", message = "No credential selected") val apiKey = executionContext.getCredential<ApiKey>(name) nodeOutputWriter.createOutputPortWriter("output").use { writer -> writer.write(0L, mapOf("key_length" to apiKey.key.length)) } } } The example only writes the length of the key. Never write secrets to an output port or a log. In your own node, use the key to call the API and write the response. Things to know: getCredential throws CredentialsNotFoundException if no credential has that name. Decide whether that should be retried; usually it is a user error and should become a non-retriable NodeRuntimeException. In Java, call executionContext.getCredential(name, ApiKey.class), with ApiKey as a class or record whose fields match the credential's keys. The execute override takes the same five parameters. Overriding the five-parameter execute replaces the four-parameter one. Don't override both. The worker reads credentials from the credentials server at CONTINUUM_CREDENTIALS_SERVER_BASE_URL (default http://localhost:8083). The template's local Docker stack doesn't include one, so you can't try this node end to end locally unless you run the credentials server yourself. Test it with a fake fetcher instead, as below. On Kubernetes, set that variable in your chart. The continuum-platform chart deploys the credentials server, but the template's deployment.yaml doesn't pass its address to your worker, so a credential node would look for localhost:8083 and fail. Add this to the env: list in charts/<repo>/templates/deployment.yaml, next to CONTINUUM_API_SERVER_BASE_URL, and adjust the host if you installed continuum-platform under another release name (the service is <release-name>-credentials-server, port 8080): - name: CONTINUUM_CREDENTIALS_SERVER_BASE_URL value: "http://continuum-platform-credentials-server:8080" For the platform side (how credentials are stored and fetched), see Credentials in the node model. Test it by giving ExecutionContext a fake CredentialFetcher: package com.acme.demo.node import org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test import org.mockito.kotlin.any import org.mockito.kotlin.argumentCaptor import org.mockito.kotlin.mock import org.mockito.kotlin.verify import org.mockito.kotlin.whenever import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.context.CredentialFetcher import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.context.ExecutionContext import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.utils.NodeOutputWriter class ApiLookupNodeModelTest { @Test fun `reads the selected credential`() { val outputWriter = mock<NodeOutputWriter>() val portWriter = mock<NodeOutputWriter.OutputPortWriter>() whenever(outputWriter.createOutputPortWriter("output")).thenReturn(portWriter) val context = ExecutionContext( ownerId = "test-user", credentialFetcher = CredentialFetcher { name -> if (name == "my-key") mapOf("key" to "abc123") else null } ) ApiLookupNodeModel().execute(mapOf("credential" to "my-key"), emptyMap(), outputWriter, mock(), context) val row = argumentCaptor<Map<String, Any>>() verify(portWriter).write(any(), row.capture()) assertEquals(6, row.firstValue["key_length"]) } }

By default a failing node is retried with the workflow's retry policy. To give one node its own policy, set retryOptions in its metadata: override val metadata = ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodeData( id = this.javaClass.name, nodeModel = this.javaClass.name, title = "API Lookup", description = "Calls an API with a stored credential", retryOptions = ContinuumWorkflowModel.RetryOptionsConfig(maximumAttempts = 3, initialIntervalSeconds = 5), // … ports, properties and schemas as before ) RetryOptionsConfig has five optional fields: initialIntervalSeconds, backoffCoefficient, maximumIntervalSeconds, maximumAttempts and doNotRetry (a list of exception type names that must never be retried). Leave a field out to keep the default. In Java, pass null for the retryOptions argument of NodeData to keep the workflow default, as the Word Counter does. A NodeRuntimeException with isRetriable = false is never retried, whatever the policy says.

The Continuum plugins already give you Spring, Jackson 3, the test libraries and SLF4J. Add anything else to the feature module's own build.gradle.kts, not the worker's: dependencies { implementation("org.apache.commons:commons-text:1.12.0") } The worker picks it up through implementation(project(":features:<repo>")). Don't add Jackson 2 artifacts; they clash with the platform's Jackson 3.

Use SLF4J. The plugins put it on the classpath, so no dependency is needed: import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory private val logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(WordCounterNodeModel::class.java) // inside execute(): logger.info("Counted words in {} rows", rowNumber) The template's application.yaml sets the root log level to error and your package to debug, so your info and debug lines show up in the worker's console while other libraries stay quiet. Don't log row contents or credentials.

Run the worker from your IDE. Start App.kt in the worker module with the debugger and set breakpoints in your node. The worker defaults match the local stack, so no extra configuration is needed. Or attach to Gradle. ./gradlew :worker:bootRun --debug-jvm waits for a debugger on port 5005. Run a workflow in the Workbench to trigger the node. A breakpoint in execute() pauses it. Temporal may time the activity out if you stay paused for a long time, so step through quickly. Prefer a unit test when you can: it reproduces most logic bugs without Docker. Add a failing test, fix the code, keep the test. Next: if something doesn't work, see Troubleshooting.

documents.t: On GitHub, open continuum-feature-template and click Use this template. That creates a copy in your own organisation without the template's git history. Then clone your copy: git clone https://github.com/<your-org>/<your-repo>.git cd <your-repo>

./gradlew build This compiles both example modules, runs their unit tests, checks that every node is annotated correctly and packages the worker jar. The Gradle wrapper is already in the repo; you only need JDK 21.

cd docker docker compose up -d Wait until docker compose ps shows the services as healthy. The temporal-search-attributes-init container exits when its setup is done; that's expected. The stack needs about 8 GB of RAM.

From the repository root: ./gradlew :worker:bootRun The worker connects to Temporal, registers its nodes with the platform and serves on port 8090. Wait for these lines in its output: Registered process nodes: [org.projectcontinuum.feature.example.node.HelloWorldNodeModel, org.projectcontinuum.feature.example.java.node.HelloJavaNodeModel]

Open the Workbench at http://localhost:3002. In the node palette, find Hello World and Hello Java under Examples. Drag a table source onto the canvas (for example Create Table), connect it to Hello World, and run the workflow. Each row gets a new greeting column. It worked if you see the nodes If the palette is empty, the worker didn't register. Check http://localhost:8090/actuator/health and see Troubleshooting.

Step 2 of 6About 5 minutes The template has about 40 files, but you will only write code in a handful of them. This page shows which ones, and why the rest exist.

Your repository builds one worker. The worker is a small Spring Boot app that loads one or more feature modules. A feature module is a Gradle library that contains your node classes. The template ships two example modules, one in Kotlin and one in Java. You keep the one you write in and delete the other in Step 3. At startup the worker finds every class annotated with @ContinuumNode, listens on its own Temporal task queue for work, and announces each node to the platform so it shows up in the Workbench palette.

Each file or folder below is tagged with what you need to do with it. Tag Meaning Write Your code goes here. You'll edit or add files. Rename once Contains the template's name. Change it in Step 3, then forget about it. Keep in sync Several files must agree. If you change one, change the others. Leave alone Works as shipped. continuum-feature-template/ ├── gradle.properties Keep in sync platform + feature versions ├── settings.gradle.kts Rename once project name + list of modules ├── build.gradle.kts Leave alone │ ├── features/ │ └── continuum-feature-hello/ Rename once a feature module (Kotlin) │ ├── build.gradle.kts Rename once group, description │ └── src/ │ ├── main/kotlin/…/example/ │ │ ├── AutoConfigure.kt Rename once tells Spring where your nodes are │ │ └── node/ │ │ └── HelloWorldNodeModel.kt Write ← your node │ ├── main/resources/ │ │ ├── META-INF/spring/…AutoConfiguration.imports Rename once │ │ └── …/node/HelloWorldNodeModel.doc.md Write ← help page │ └── test/kotlin/…/HelloWorldNodeModelTest.kt Write ← unit test │ ├── features/continuum-feature-hello-java/ Rename once same layout in Java; delete whichever example you don't need │ ├── worker/ │ ├── build.gradle.kts Keep in sync which modules the worker loads, image name │ └── src/main/ │ ├── kotlin/…/App.kt Leave alone Spring Boot entry point │ └── resources/application.yaml Keep in sync task queue, app name │ ├── charts/continuum-feature-template/ Keep in sync Helm chart for Kubernetes ├── docker/ Leave alone local Continuum stack ├── .github/workflows/ Keep in sync CI and release (lists your modules) └── README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, AGENTS.md Rename once still describe the template

These three live side by side in each feature module and share a name. The Java module has the same layout, with HelloJavaNodeModel and .java files: File What it is node/HelloWorldNodeModel.kt The node: ports, settings form and the execute() logic. resources/…/node/HelloWorldNodeModel.doc.md The help page the Workbench shows next to the node. The path must match the class's package and name exactly. test/…/HelloWorldNodeModelTest.kt Unit test. Runs without Spring, Kafka or Docker.

If you get one of the first three wrong, the build still passes but the worker starts with no nodes, and nothing in the build output tells you why. These are the most common reasons a new node doesn't appear. File Why it matters AutoConfigure.kt A small @Configuration + @ComponentScan class. It makes Spring scan your package for nodes. Your node classes must live in this package or below. If basePackages doesn't cover your node's package, the node isn't found. META-INF/spring/…AutoConfiguration.imports One line naming the AutoConfigure class. Spring Boot reads this file to find your module. If the file is missing or names the wrong class, Spring doesn't load your module. worker/build.gradle.kts Its implementation(project(...)) lines decide which feature modules the worker loads. A module that isn't listed here is never loaded. node/ package name Node classes belong in a package ending in .node. The platform derives your feature ID by removing that last segment. (Other package names still load; the feature ID is then the whole package.) If a node doesn't appear after Step 5, follow the checklist in Troubleshooting.

documents.t: Setting Where it lives Rule Task queue worker/src/main/resources/application.yaml and taskQueue in charts/*/values.yaml Must be unique across all workers and identical in both files. Two workers on one queue means Temporal can hand a node to a worker that doesn't have it. featureVersion gradle.properties and appVersion in charts/*/Chart.yaml Must be equal. CI fails otherwise. continuumPlatformVersion gradle.properties only Every module reads it with property(...). Never hardcode it in a build file. Module list settings.gradle.kts, worker/build.gradle.kts and .github/workflows/on-release.yml + build-module.yml Add or rename a module in all four.
documents.s: Files that must agree with each other

documents.t: docker/: the local stack from Step 1. It has nothing of yours in it. gradlew, gradle/: the Gradle wrapper. App.kt: three lines that start Spring Boot. charts/…/templates/: Helm templates. You only touch them to rename (Step 3).

You don't declare Spring, Temporal, Jackson or test dependencies. The three Continuum plugins add them: Plugin Used in Gives you org.projectcontinuum.feature feature modules Kotlin, Spring dependency management, continuum-commons, test libraries, and the validateContinuumNodeAnnotations check that fails the build if a node lacks @ContinuumNode. org.projectcontinuum.feature-java Java feature modules The same, for Java. org.projectcontinuum.worker worker/ Spring Boot, the worker starter (Temporal polling and node registration), bootRun, and Jib for the container image. Add a dependencies { } block to a feature module only when your node needs an extra library; see Add a library. The plugin versions are the continuumPlatformVersion in gradle.properties (see the version note in the overview). Next: rename the template.
documents.s: What the Gradle plugins do for you

documents.t: Step 3 of 6About 5 minutes with the script, 20 by hand The template carries its own name in many files. This step replaces it with yours and removes the example module in the language you don't use. It's mechanical, and you only do it once. You have two ways to do it: run a script that does the whole job, or work through the manual checklist. Both end at the same leftover check.

Pick these first, and check the other Continuum repositories to make sure the names aren't already in use: Placeholder Example Used for Changing it later <org> acme Your GitHub organisation or user, and your Docker Hub organisation Easy. <repo> continuum-feature-demo Repository, Gradle root project, feature module, Helm chart, worker and Docker image name Possible, but you repeat this whole step. <package> com.acme.demo Package for your nodes (the node classes go in <package>.node) Breaks saved workflows that use your nodes, because the package is part of each node's identity. Don't change it after shipping. <TASK_QUEUE> CONTINUUM_FEATURE_DEMO_TASK_QUEUE Temporal task queue. Must be unique across all workers in your Continuum instance. Change it in application.yaml and the chart together. <valuesKey> featureDemo The key under continuum: in the Helm chart's values Easy, but change it in every chart file. Pick a package you own Use a package that starts with a domain you control (com.acme.demo) or io.github.<your-user>. Don't use org.projectcontinuum.*: that namespace belongs to the platform. The feature module's Maven group is set to your package, and Maven Central only accepts a group whose namespace you've verified. If you don't plan to publish your feature modules as libraries, you can ignore this and switch publishing off in Step 6. Pick a unique task queue now Every worker needs its own task queue. If two workers share one, Temporal gives a node's work to whichever worker polls first, including one that doesn't have that node, and the node fails at random. Search the other Continuum repositories before you pick a name.

The template ships the same Hello World node twice: features/continuum-feature-hello (Kotlin) and features/continuum-feature-hello-java (Java). Keep the one that matches the language you write and delete the other. Mixing languages in one module isn't supported by the template; if you want both, keep both modules and run through the checklist for each.

The script below does everything in Option B except editing the descriptions and the README. It's been tested on a fresh clone of the template for both the Kotlin and the Java variants, followed by ./gradlew build. Commit or stash anything you changed so you can review the result with git diff. Save the script as rename.sh outside the repository (for example in your home folder). Edit the six values at the top, including LANGUAGE. Run it from anywhere inside your clone: bash ~/rename.sh. It needs bash and perl, which macOS and Linux have. On Windows, use WSL or Git Bash. rename.sh #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail # ---- Edit these six values --------------------------------------------- export ORG=acme # your GitHub organisation or user export REPO=continuum-feature-demo # repository, module, chart and worker name export PKG=com.acme.demo # package for your nodes (without .node) export TASK_QUEUE=CONTINUUM_FEATURE_DEMO_TASK_QUEUE export VALUES_KEY=featureDemo # key under `continuum:` in the Helm values export IMAGE=acme/continuum-feature-demo # Docker image, without a tag LANGUAGE=kotlin # kotlin or java: which example module to keep # ------------------------------------------------------------------------- cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" if [ "$LANGUAGE" = kotlin ]; then KEEP=continuum-feature-hello export OLD_PKG=org.projectcontinuum.feature.example export DROP_RE='continuum-feature-hello-java' export DROP_PLUGIN='id\("org\.projectcontinuum\.feature-java"\)' DROP=continuum-feature-hello-java else KEEP=continuum-feature-hello-java export OLD_PKG=org.projectcontinuum.feature.example.java export DROP_RE='continuum-feature-hello(?!-java)' export DROP_PLUGIN='id\("org\.projectcontinuum\.feature"\)' DROP=continuum-feature-hello fi export SHORT="${REPO#continuum-}" OLD_PATH="${OLD_PKG//.//}" NEW_PATH="${PKG//.//}" # 1. Remove the example module you don't need rm -rf "features/$DROP" perl -ni -e 'print unless /$ENV{DROP_RE}/' \ settings.gradle.kts worker/build.gradle.kts .github/workflows/build-module.yml perl -ni -e 'print unless /$ENV{DROP_PLUGIN}/' settings.gradle.kts perl -0pi -e 's/^ *- module: features:$ENV{DROP_RE}\n(?: +publish_\w+: \w+\n)+//m' \ .github/workflows/on-release.yml # 2. Rename the module, package folders and chart folder mv "features/$KEEP" "features/$REPO" for d in src/main/kotlin src/main/java src/main/resources src/test/kotlin src/test/java; do src="features/$REPO/$d/$OLD_PATH" if [ -d "$src" ]; then mkdir -p "features/$REPO/$d/$(dirname "$NEW_PATH")" mv "$src" "features/$REPO/$d/$NEW_PATH" fi done find "features/$REPO" -type d -empty -delete mv charts/continuum-feature-template "charts/$REPO" # 3. Replace the template's names inside files find . \( -name .git -o -name .gradle -o -name .kotlin -o -name build -o -name .idea \ -o -path ./docker -o -path ./gradle \) -prune -o -type f ! -name 'gradlew*' -print0 | xargs -0 perl -pi -e ' s{org\.projectcontinuum\.feature\.example(\.java)?}{$ENV{PKG}}g; s{projectcontinuum/continuum-feature-template}{$ENV{IMAGE}}g; s{projectcontinuum-org/continuum-feature-template}{$ENV{ORG}/$ENV{REPO}}g; s{continuum-feature-hello(-java)?}{$ENV{REPO}}g; s{continuum-feature-template}{$ENV{REPO}}g; s{CONTINUUM_FEATURE_TEMPLATE_TASK_QUEUE}{$ENV{TASK_QUEUE}}g; s{featureTemplate}{$ENV{VALUES_KEY}}g; s{feature-template}{$ENV{SHORT}}g; ' perl -pi -e 's{org\.projectcontinuum\.app\.worker\.example}{$ENV{PKG}.app.worker}g' worker/build.gradle.kts echo "Done. Still to do by hand: the description lines in build.gradle.kts and Chart.yaml, and README.md." echo "Leftovers (expect none):" grep -rIn "feature-template\|featureTemplate\|FEATURE_TEMPLATE\|feature\.example\|feature-hello" \ --exclude-dir=.git --exclude-dir=.gradle --exclude-dir=.kotlin --exclude-dir=build . || true When it finishes, the "Leftovers" list at the end of its output should be empty. Then finish by hand: The description lines in features/<repo>/build.gradle.kts, worker/build.gradle.kts and charts/<repo>/Chart.yaml. The script renames words but can't rewrite a sentence. README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md and AGENTS.md: the script fixes names and links, but the text still describes the template (badges, the "Ownership" list in AGENTS.md, and so on). Rewrite what no longer applies. Skip ahead to Check for leftovers.

documents.t: Work through this in order and commit when the build is green. <example-module> below means the module you keep: continuum-feature-hello (Kotlin) or continuum-feature-hello-java (Java).
settings.gradle.kts: set rootProject.name = "<repo>". gradle.properties: set repoName=<org>/<repo>. Leave the version lines as they are.

Delete the other module's folder under features/. Remove its include(...) line from settings.gradle.kts. Remove its implementation(project(...)) line from worker/build.gradle.kts. settings.gradle.kts also declares the Gradle plugins in pluginManagement { plugins { … } }. Remove the id("org.projectcontinuum.feature-java") line if you keep Kotlin, or the id("org.projectcontinuum.feature") line if you keep Java. .github/workflows/on-release.yml: delete its - module: entry in the matrix, including the publish_* lines under it. .github/workflows/build-module.yml: delete its line in the options: list.
documents.s: 2. Remove the example you don't need

documents.t: Rename the folder features/<example-module>/ to features/<repo>/ and then: settings.gradle.kts: change include(":features:<example-module>") to include(":features:<repo>"). features/<repo>/build.gradle.kts: change group to <package> and rewrite description. Rename the package folders under src/main/kotlin (or src/main/java), src/test/… and src/main/resources. The old path is org/projectcontinuum/feature/example for Kotlin and org/projectcontinuum/feature/example/java for Java. Replace it with your <package> path. Update the package line in every file you moved. AutoConfigure.kt (or AutoConfigure.java): update the basePackages value in @ComponentScan to <package>. META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports: change the line to <package>.AutoConfigure. Use your IDE's rename In IntelliJ, use Refactor → Rename on the package and module folders. It updates package lines and imports for you. You still have to edit basePackages, the .imports file and the Gradle files by hand.

worker/build.gradle.kts: implementation(project(":features:<repo>")) must point at your renamed module. Change jibToImage to the image you will publish, for example <org>/<repo>:${project.version}. Change group and description. worker/src/main/resources/application.yaml: spring.application.name → <repo>-worker the default of node-task-queue → <TASK_QUEUE> the org.projectcontinuum.feature.example log level → <package>

The chart folder, its helper templates and its values keys all carry the template's name. Replace them together or Helm will fail with "template not found". Rename charts/continuum-feature-template/ to charts/<repo>/. Chart.yaml: change name, description and home. values.yaml and values-dev.yaml: the featureTemplate: key → <valuesKey> image.repository → your image from jibToImage taskQueue → <TASK_QUEUE> (the same value as in application.yaml) templates/*.yaml, templates/_helpers.tpl and templates/NOTES.txt: replace every continuum-feature-template with <repo>, every .featureTemplate. with .<valuesKey>., and the feature-template component label with your own. Chart.yaml appVersion must equal featureVersion in gradle.properties (both 0.0.1 as shipped).
.github/workflows/on-release.yml: update the module: entry for your module in the matrix. .github/workflows/build-module.yml: update the options: list to your module name.
README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md and AGENTS.md: replace the template's name, badges, links and descriptions.

Run this from the repository root. It prints nothing when every rename is done: grep -rIn "feature-template\|featureTemplate\|FEATURE_TEMPLATE\|feature\.example\|feature-hello" \ --exclude-dir=.git --exclude-dir=.gradle --exclude-dir=.kotlin --exclude-dir=build . Any line it prints is a missed rename. (AGENTS.md and README.md are the files most often missed.) Then confirm nothing broke: ./gradlew build If you changed the chart, also run helm lint charts/<repo>. At this point the build contains the template's Hello World node under your name. That's expected: you replace it in the next step.

The module folder, the include(...) line in settings.gradle.kts and the implementation(project(...)) line in worker/build.gradle.kts all use the same module name. The .imports file names your real AutoConfigure class. node-task-queue in application.yaml equals taskQueue in the chart's values.yaml. featureVersion in gradle.properties equals appVersion in Chart.yaml. The leftover grep above prints nothing. ./gradlew build passes, and helm lint charts/<repo> passes. What you can skip for now You can postpone the Helm chart and the workflow files until you are ready to deploy (Step 6). The build, tests and local run only need the project, module and worker sections. If you postpone them, the leftover grep will still report the chart and workflows. Next: write your node.

Step 4 of 6About 30 minutes You don't start from a blank file. Take the template's Hello World node (or Hello Java) and rewrite it into your own: rename the files and the class, then replace the ports, settings and logic. The running example here is a Word Counter that counts the words in a text column and appends the count as a new column. Every code sample on this page was compiled and its tests were run against platform 0.0.20. Pick your language in the tabs; the choice sticks across the page. A node is three files that share a name. Do them in this order: The node class The help page The unit test Once those work, More node recipes shows how to add a second node, write a source node, use credentials and more.

Rename HelloWorldNodeModel.kt (Java: HelloJavaNodeModel.java) to WordCounterNodeModel.kt (or .java) and the class inside it, then replace the contents. The class has six parts: @ContinuumNode ← required, never remove class WordCounterNodeModel : ProcessNodeModel() { 1. ports what goes in and out 2. categories where it appears in the palette 3. propertiesSchema what settings exist, and what is valid 4. propertiesUiSchema how the settings form looks 5. metadata name, description, icon, defaults 6. execute() the logic } Here is the finished Word Counter, with the six parts marked. It lives in the package <package>.node, which is com.acme.demo.node in this example: Kotlin Java package com.acme.demo.node import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.annotation.ContinuumNode import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.exception.NodeRuntimeException import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.model.ContinuumWorkflowModel import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.node.ProcessNodeModel import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.protocol.progress.NodeProgressCallback import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.utils.NodeInputReader import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.utils.NodeOutputWriter import org.springframework.http.MediaType.APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE import tools.jackson.core.type.TypeReference import tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper @ContinuumNode class WordCounterNodeModel( private val objectMapper: ObjectMapper ) : ProcessNodeModel() { private val whitespace = Regex("\\s+") // 1. Ports. The map keys ("input", "output") are the port IDs you use in execute(). final override val inputPorts = mapOf( "input" to ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort(name = "Input Table", contentType = APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE) ) final override val outputPorts = mapOf( "output" to ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort(name = "Table with word counts", contentType = APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE) ) // 2. Palette category override val categories = listOf("Demo") // 3. JSON Schema: the settings and their rules private val propertiesSchema: Map<String, Any> = objectMapper.readValue( """ { "type": "object", "properties": { "inputCol": { "type": "string", "title": "Input Column" }, "outputCol": { "type": "string", "title": "Output Column" }, "minWordLength": { "type": "integer", "title": "Minimum Word Length", "minimum": 1, "default": 1 } }, "required": ["inputCol", "outputCol"] } """.trimIndent(), object : TypeReference<Map<String, Any>>() {} ) // 4. JSON Forms UI schema: the layout of the settings form private val propertiesUiSchema: Map<String, Any> = objectMapper.readValue( """ { "type": "VerticalLayout", "elements": [ { "type": "Control", "scope": "#/properties/inputCol" }, { "type": "Control", "scope": "#/properties/outputCol" }, { "type": "Control", "scope": "#/properties/minWordLength" } ] } """.trimIndent(), object : TypeReference<Map<String, Any>>() {} ) // 5. Metadata: what the Workbench and the registry see override val metadata = ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodeData( id = this.javaClass.name, nodeModel = this.javaClass.name, title = "Word Counter", subTitle = "Count words per row", description = "Counts the words in a text column and appends the count as a new column", icon = """<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" d="M4 6h16M4 12h10M4 18h6M18 14v6m-3-3h6"/></svg>""", inputs = inputPorts, outputs = outputPorts, properties = mapOf("inputCol" to "text", "outputCol" to "word_count", "minWordLength" to 1), propertiesSchema = propertiesSchema, propertiesUISchema = propertiesUiSchema ) // 6. The logic override fun execute( properties: Map<String, Any>?, inputs: Map<String, NodeInputReader>, nodeOutputWriter: NodeOutputWriter, nodeProgressCallback: NodeProgressCallback ) { val inputCol = properties?.get("inputCol") as String? ?: throw NodeRuntimeException(isRetriable = false, workflowId = "", nodeId = "", message = "inputCol is not provided") val outputCol = properties["outputCol"] as String? ?: throw NodeRuntimeException(isRetriable = false, workflowId = "", nodeId = "", message = "outputCol is not provided") val minWordLength = (properties["minWordLength"] as Number?)?.toInt() ?: 1 val reader = inputs["input"] ?: throw NodeRuntimeException( isRetriable = false, workflowId = "", nodeId = "", message = "Input port 'input' is not connected" ) val totalRows = reader.getRowCount() nodeOutputWriter.createOutputPortWriter("output").use { writer -> reader.use { var rowNumber = 0L while (true) { val row = reader.read() ?: break val text = row[inputCol]?.toString() ?: "" val count = text.trim().split(whitespace).count { it.length >= minWordLength } writer.write(rowNumber, row.toMutableMap().apply { this[outputCol] = count }) rowNumber++ if (totalRows > 0) nodeProgressCallback.report((rowNumber * 100 / totalRows).toInt()) } } } } } package com.acme.demo.node; import org.jetbrains.annotations.NotNull; import org.jetbrains.annotations.Nullable; import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.annotation.ContinuumNode; import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.exception.NodeRuntimeException; import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.model.ContinuumWorkflowModel; import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.node.ProcessNodeModel; import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.protocol.progress.NodeProgressCallback; import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.utils.NodeInputReader; import org.projectcontinuum.core.commons.utils.NodeOutputWriter; import org.springframework.http.MediaType; import tools.jackson.core.type.TypeReference; import tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; @ContinuumNode public class WordCounterNodeModel extends ProcessNodeModel { private static final ObjectMapper MAPPER = new ObjectMapper(); private static final TypeReference<Map<String, Object>> MAP_TYPE = new TypeReference<>() {}; // 1. Ports. The map keys ("input", "output") are the port IDs you use in execute(). private final Map<String, ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort> inputPorts = Map.of( "input", new ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort("Input Table", MediaType.APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE)); private final Map<String, ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort> outputPorts = Map.of( "output", new ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort("Table with word counts", MediaType.APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE)); @NotNull @Override public Map<String, ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort> getInputPorts() { return inputPorts; } @NotNull @Override public Map<String, ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort> getOutputPorts() { return outputPorts; } // 2. Palette category @NotNull @Override public List<String> getCategories() { return List.of("Demo"); } // 3. JSON Schema: the settings and their rules private static final Map<String, Object> PROPERTIES_SCHEMA = MAPPER.readValue(""" { "type": "object", "properties": { "inputCol": { "type": "string", "title": "Input Column" }, "outputCol": { "type": "string", "title": "Output Column" }, "minWordLength": { "type": "integer", "title": "Minimum Word Length", "minimum": 1, "default": 1 } }, "required": ["inputCol", "outputCol"] } """, MAP_TYPE); // 4. JSON Forms UI schema: the layout of the settings form private static final Map<String, Object> PROPERTIES_UI_SCHEMA = MAPPER.readValue(""" { "type": "VerticalLayout", "elements": [ { "type": "Control", "scope": "#/properties/inputCol" }, { "type": "Control", "scope": "#/properties/outputCol" }, { "type": "Control", "scope": "#/properties/minWordLength" } ] } """, MAP_TYPE); // 5. Metadata. Java has no default arguments, so pass all 15 parameters in order. private final ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodeData metadata = new ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodeData( getClass().getName(), // id "Counts the words in a text column and appends the count as a new column", // description "Word Counter", // title "Count words per row", // subTitle null, // icon (SVG string, or null) getClass().getName(), // nodeModel null, // busy inputPorts, // inputs outputPorts, // outputs Map.of("inputCol", "text", "outputCol", "word_count", "minWordLength", 1), // default settings PROPERTIES_SCHEMA, // propertiesSchema PROPERTIES_UI_SCHEMA, // propertiesUISchema null, // status null, // nodeProgress null // retryOptions (null = workflow default) ); @NotNull @Override public ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodeData getMetadata() { return metadata; } // 6. The logic @Override public void execute( @Nullable Map<String, ? extends Object> properties, @NotNull Map<String, NodeInputReader> inputs, @NotNull NodeOutputWriter nodeOutputWriter, @NotNull NodeProgressCallback nodeProgressCallback ) { String inputCol = requireString(properties, "inputCol"); String outputCol = requireString(properties, "outputCol"); Object min = properties.get("minWordLength"); int minWordLength = (min instanceof Number n) ? n.intValue() : 1; NodeInputReader reader = inputs.get("input"); if (reader == null) { throw new NodeRuntimeException(false, "", "", "Input port 'input' is not connected"); } long totalRows = reader.getRowCount(); long rowNumber = 0; NodeOutputWriter.OutputPortWriter writer = nodeOutputWriter.createOutputPortWriter("output"); try { Map<String, Object> row; while ((row = reader.read()) != null) { Object cell = row.get(inputCol); String text = cell == null ? "" : cell.toString().trim(); int count = 0; if (!text.isEmpty()) { for (String word : text.split("\\s+")) { if (word.length() >= minWordLength) count++; } } Map<String, Object> out = new HashMap<>(row); out.put(outputCol, count); writer.write(rowNumber, out); rowNumber++; if (totalRows > 0) nodeProgressCallback.report((int) (rowNumber * 100 / totalRows)); } } finally { writer.close(); reader.close(); } } private static String requireString(Map<String, ?> properties, String key) { Object value = properties == null ? null : properties.get(key); if (!(value instanceof String s)) { throw new NodeRuntimeException(false, "", "", key + " is not provided"); } return s; } } In Java the three overrides getInputPorts(), getOutputPorts() and getCategories() replace Kotlin's override val properties, and the @NotNull / @Nullable annotations match the Kotlin signatures. The 15 arguments to NodeData are in the order shown by the comments.

Break one of these and the build fails, the node doesn't load, or workflows break later. Rule Why Annotate with @ContinuumNode, not @Component. It makes the bean prototype-scoped, so each run gets a fresh instance. The build fails without it (validateContinuumNodeAnnotations). Extend ProcessNodeModel (has inputs) or TriggerNodeModel (source node, outputs only). TriggerNodeModel.execute() has no inputs parameter. See a source node. Set metadata.id and metadata.nodeModel to the class's full name (this.javaClass.name / getClass().getName()). The full class name is the node's identity in saved workflows. Renaming or moving the class later breaks workflows that use it. Put the class in a package that ends in .node. By convention. The platform removes that last segment to get the feature ID (com.acme.demo.node → com.acme.demo). Without it, the whole package name becomes the feature ID, and the node still loads. Import Jackson from tools.jackson.*. The platform uses Jackson 3. com.fasterxml.jackson.* (Jackson 2) won't compile. Two notes on ObjectMapper: In Kotlin you can take it as a constructor parameter and Spring injects it. In unit tests, pass jacksonObjectMapper(). In Java, the example creates a static mapper, which works because the schemas are built once when the class loads. You can also take an ObjectMapper in a constructor, as in Kotlin. If you'd rather not parse JSON strings at all, you can write the schemas as nested mapOf(...) / Map.of(...) values. The source node recipe does that.

inputPorts and outputPorts are maps: The key (here "input" and "output") is the port ID you use in execute() to read or write data. The template's Hello World node uses the same two IDs, so the rest of the platform's examples look familiar. The value is a ContinuumWorkflowModel.NodePort with a name (shown in the Workbench) and a contentType. Table ports use APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE, as in the running example. The template's example nodes do the same. A node can have several ports. Add more entries to the map, give each a different key, and use those keys in inputs["…"] and createOutputPortWriter("…"). A node with two inputs (for example "left" and "right") gets both readers in the inputs map; check each key you need, because a port that isn't connected is missing from the map.

properties in the metadata holds the default values used when a user drops the node on the canvas. Before execute() runs, the platform checks the user's settings against propertiesSchema. Values that break required, type or minimum fail the node before your code starts. Checking again in execute() is still worthwhile because it lets you give a clearer error message. propertiesUiSchema is a JSON Forms layout, used only to draw the form. For credential pickers, see Credentials. You can try schemas in the JSON Forms playground first.

inputs["input"] is a NodeInputReader. read() returns the next row as a Map<String, Any>, or null at the end. If a port isn't connected, its key is missing from inputs. createOutputPortWriter("output") returns a writer. write(rowNumber, row) takes a Long row number that starts at 0. Close both when you are done: Kotlin's .use { } or Java's try { … } finally { … }. The output file is only complete once the writer is closed. Cell values must be one of these types, and never null. Anything else makes write() throw IllegalArgumentException: Unsupported type. Leave a key out instead of storing null. Kotlin / Java type Stored as String application/vnd.continuum.x-string Int, Long application/vnd.continuum.x-int, x-long Float, Double application/vnd.continuum.x-float, x-double Boolean application/vnd.continuum.x-boolean List<*>, Map<*, *> application/json SVG org.w3c.dom.Document image/svg+xml Convert anything else first. For example, call toString() on a LocalDate, and convert a BigDecimal to a Double or a String.

Every node runs as a Temporal activity, so an exception thrown from execute() is retried by default (with exponential backoff). Throw NodeRuntimeException(isRetriable = false, ...) (Java: new NodeRuntimeException(false, "", "", message)) for errors a retry can't fix, such as: Missing or invalid settings (user error) An unconnected input port Invalid input data that can't be recovered from Empty strings are fine for workflowId and nodeId in the exception. To change the retry behaviour of one node, see per-node retry options. Call nodeProgressCallback.report(percent) (0 to 100) as you go. The Workbench shows it as live progress on the node.

Rename HelloWorldNodeModel.doc.md (Java: HelloJavaNodeModel.doc.md) to WordCounterNodeModel.doc.md and rewrite it. The Workbench shows this file next to the node. The path must match the node's package and class name exactly. For the class com.acme.demo.node.WordCounterNodeModel, the file is: src/main/resources/com/acme/demo/node/WordCounterNodeModel.doc.md To build the path, take the class's full name, replace each . with / and add .doc.md. The node folder is part of the package, not an extra segment. If the file is missing or misplaced, the node still works, but its help page reads "Documentation not found for WordCounterNodeModel", and the build doesn't warn you. A good help page has four parts, as in the template's Hello World page: what the node does, a Configuration table, a Ports table, and a small Example with input and output tables.

Rename HelloWorldNodeModelTest.kt (Java: HelloJavaNodeModelTest.java) to WordCounterNodeModelTest.kt (or .java). Nodes are plain classes, so you can test execute() with Mockito mocks. To test validation as well, build a ContinuumWorkflowModel.Node and call node.run(...) instead. Next: test and run your node.
Step 5 of 6About 10 minutes You ran the template unchanged in Step 1. Now run it again with your changes.
documents.s: Step 5: Test and run your node

documents.t: ./gradlew build This compiles every module, runs your unit tests, runs validateContinuumNodeAnnotations and builds the worker jar. To run one test class: ./gradlew :features:<repo>:test --tests "*WordCounterNodeModelTest" The annotation check validateContinuumNodeAnnotations fails the build when a class extends ProcessNodeModel or TriggerNodeModel without @ContinuumNode. If you see it fail, that's the cause.
Make sure the local stack from Step 1 is still up (docker compose ps in docker/), then: ./gradlew :worker:bootRun

The worker logs every node it found when it starts. Look for these two lines in the bootRun output: Registered process nodes: [com.acme.demo.node.WordCounterNodeModel] Registered trigger nodes: [] Your node's full class name should be in the list. You can also ask the worker over HTTP: curl http://localhost:8090/api/v1/node-repo Your Word Counter should be in the response. If it isn't, the build passed but the worker didn't find your node. Work through the checklist in Troubleshooting. Most often, one of these is wrong: the module isn't listed in worker/build.gradle.kts, the .imports file names the wrong class or @ComponentScan doesn't cover your package. (A missing @ContinuumNode is rarely the cause, because the build catches it.)

Open http://localhost:3002. Word Counter appears under Demo. Add a table source that has a text column, such as Create Table, and connect it to Word Counter. Open the Word Counter settings to see the form you defined, then run the workflow. Click the output port. Every row has a new word_count column. Open the node's help page in the Workbench. It should show your .doc.md content. If it reads "Documentation not found", see Step 4. Locally you don't need to set any environment variables: the worker's defaults match the local stack. When you deploy elsewhere, see the worker configuration reference. You've now changed the template into your own working worker. Next: ship it.
Step 6 of 6Needs repository secrets Shipping is mostly already set up in the template. This page explains what each piece does, what you need to provide and how to install the result.
Publish a GitHub Release After merging to main, create a release in the GitHub UI. That is what starts the publishing workflows.

Every change under features/ or worker/ needs: A new featureVersion in gradle.properties The chart's appVersion in charts/<repo>/Chart.yaml set to the same value CI enforces both on every pull request (validate-versions.yml). If your PR fails with "does not match featureVersion" or "featureVersion must be bumped", this is why. Example: # gradle.properties featureVersion=0.0.2 # charts/<repo>/Chart.yaml appVersion: "0.0.2" # Must match gradle.properties The Docker image tag defaults to the chart's appVersion, so the chart installs exactly the image built from the same release.

Workflow When What it does ci.yml PR, push to main ./gradlew build validate-versions.yml PR Checks the version rules above lint-test.yml PR touching charts/ ct lint on the Helm chart build-module.yml Manual Build one module, optionally publish it on-release.yml GitHub release published Libraries → Maven Central, worker → Docker Hub release.yml GitHub release published Attach the packaged Helm chart to the release and update the gh-pages index Workflows are triggered by a published release on-release.yml and release.yml run when you publish a GitHub Release (Repository → Releases → Create a new release). Pushing a tag or merging to main doesn't trigger them.

The release workflows read these from your repository's Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions: Secret Used for Required? MAVEN_CENTRAL_USERNAME, MAVEN_CENTRAL_PASSWORD Publishing libraries to Maven Central If publishing to Maven Central GPG_KEY_ID, GPG_PASSPHRASE, GPG_SECRET_KEY, GPG_PUBLIC_KEY Signing the published artifacts If publishing to Maven Central DOCKER_HUB_USERNAME, DOCKER_HUB_PASSWORD Pushing the worker image Yes, unless you change the image registry (see below)

Maven Central only accepts artifacts whose group is a namespace you have verified in the Central Portal. Your feature module's group is your <package> (for example com.acme.demo), so verify com.acme.demo's parent domain (com.acme) or use io.github.<your-user>. The Central Portal's namespace documentation explains the DNS or GitHub proof. Not publishing libraries? If your nodes only run in your own worker, you don't need Maven Central or the GPG secrets, and you don't need a verified namespace. Do both of these: In each feature module's continuum { } block, add publishToMavenCentral.set(false). In .github/workflows/on-release.yml, set publish_to_maven: false for those modules. Otherwise the release workflow tries to publish and fails on the missing secrets or namespace.

The worker image is built with Jib, so you don't need a Dockerfile and the CI runner doesn't need Docker. The target is jibToImage in worker/build.gradle.kts: continuum { continuumVersion.set(continuumPlatformVersion) jibToImage.set("acme/continuum-feature-demo:${project.version}") } on-release.yml runs ./gradlew :worker:jib, which pushes that image using the DOCKER_REPO_USERNAME and DOCKER_REPO_PASSWORD environment variables. The workflow fills them from DOCKER_HUB_USERNAME and DOCKER_HUB_PASSWORD. To use another registry (GitHub Container Registry, a private registry), put its full address in jibToImage (for example ghcr.io/acme/continuum-feature-demo:${project.version}), keep the same environment variable names, and change the env: lines of the "Push container image" step in on-release.yml to read your registry's credentials. Also change image.repository in the chart's values.yaml to match. If the registry is private, your cluster needs a pull secret. The template chart's global.imagePullSecrets value exists, but the Deployment template doesn't use it yet. Add this under spec.template.spec in charts/<repo>/templates/deployment.yaml: {{- with .Values.global.imagePullSecrets }} imagePullSecrets: {{- toYaml . | nindent 8 }} {{- end }} Then create the secret in the namespace (kubectl create secret docker-registry …) and list it in values.yaml: global: imagePullSecrets: - name: my-registry-secret

The chart wires your worker to the rest of the platform through the continuum: block in values.yaml. Three parts of it need your attention: Values What it is When to change it continuum.infra.* Addresses of the shared services: Temporal (host, port, namespace), Kafka (brokerList), the schema registry (url) and MinIO (endpoint). If you didn't install the continuum-infra chart under its default release name continuum-infra. Each address contains that release name. continuum.secrets.existingMinioSecret The name of the Kubernetes Secret that holds MinIO's root-user and root-password. Your chart doesn't create it; the continuum-platform chart does, named <release-name>-minio-secret. If you installed continuum-platform under a name other than continuum-platform. continuum.apiServer host and port of the platform's API server, where your worker registers its nodes. The default is the service continuum-platform-api-server on port 8080. Same: if the release name differs. Find the real service and secret names in your cluster with: kubectl get svc,secret -n continuum Your worker's own settings are under continuum.<valuesKey> (image, replicas, taskQueue, resources, autoscaling).

Before installing the chart, check the points that must agree: taskQueue in charts/<repo>/values.yaml matches node-task-queue in application.yaml taskQueue is globally unique (search other workers) image.repository in values.yaml matches what your release pushes The continuum.infra.*, secrets.existingMinioSecret and apiServer values match the release names in your cluster (see above) helm lint charts/<repo> passes

You can install from your working copy, or from the chart your release published. From the repository (good for a first test): helm install <repo> ./charts/<repo> -n continuum From your release: the release.yml workflow attaches the packaged chart (<repo>-<version>.tgz) to the GitHub release and adds it to the Helm index on your gh-pages branch. Enable GitHub Pages for the gh-pages branch in your repository settings (Settings → Pages), then: helm repo add <repo> https://<org>.github.io/<repo> helm repo update helm install <repo> <repo>/<repo> -n continuum For a private repository the index isn't publicly readable. Download the .tgz from the release and run helm install <repo> ./<repo>-0.0.2.tgz -n continuum instead. To roll out a new version, publish a new release and run helm upgrade. See Deployment for the full Kubernetes setup, and confirm the result by looking for your nodes in the Workbench, or check the worker's log for Registered process nodes: [...].

You don't need to set Kafka, MinIO or the API server addresses locally; the worker starter ships defaults that match the local stack. In Kubernetes, the chart sets these for you from values.yaml. Override them with environment variables when you deploy some other way: Variable Default Purpose CONTINUUM_NODE_TASK_QUEUE from application.yaml This worker's Temporal task queue TEMPORAL_SERVER_ADDRESS localhost:7233 Temporal frontend TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE default Temporal namespace CONTINUUM_API_SERVER_BASE_URL http://localhost:8080 Where nodes register CONTINUUM_KAFKA_MAIN_BROKER_LIST localhost:39092,localhost:39093,localhost:39094 Kafka brokers CONTINUUM_KAFKA_MAIN_SCHEMA_REGISTRY http://localhost:38080 Schema registry CONTINUUM_MINIO_ENDPOINT http://localhost:39000 Object storage for node data CONTINUUM_MINIO_USERNAME / _PASSWORD minioadmin MinIO credentials CONTINUUM_CREDENTIALS_SERVER_BASE_URL http://localhost:8083 Only for nodes that call getCredential(). The template chart doesn't set it; see Use a credential. CONTINUUM_CACHE_STORAGE_PATH ./.continuum-cache/workflow-data Local scratch folder SERVER_PORT 8090 Worker HTTP port (8080 belongs to the API server) You're done. Your worker is live and its nodes are available in the Workbench.

The build passes but your node isn't in the palette. Work down this list in order. Did the worker find the node? Look at the bootRun output for the line Registered process nodes: [...] (or Registered trigger nodes: [...] for a source node). If your class is listed, the worker is fine and the problem is on the Workbench or platform side: refresh the page and check that the local stack is healthy (docker compose ps in docker/). If the list is empty or your class is missing, continue with the checks below. Is the worker registered with the API server? Open http://localhost:8090/actuator/health, then run curl http://localhost:8090/api/v1/node-repo. The worker must be able to reach the API server (CONTINUUM_API_SERVER_BASE_URL, default http://localhost:8080). Is the module on the worker? worker/build.gradle.kts needs implementation(project(":features:<repo>")): grep "implementation(project" worker/build.gradle.kts Does the .imports file name your AutoConfigure class? The file is in your feature module, not the worker: cat features/<repo>/src/main/resources/META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports It must contain exactly <your.package>.AutoConfigure. Does @ComponentScan cover your node? In features/<repo>/src/main/kotlin/<your/package/path>/AutoConfigure.kt (or src/main/java/…/AutoConfigure.java), basePackages must include your node's package. The node class must be in that package or below. Is the class annotated? It needs @ContinuumNode, not @Component. ./gradlew build fails without it (validateContinuumNodeAnnotations), so if the build passed, this is rarely the cause. After fixing any of these, rebuild and restart the worker. Reloading the browser isn't enough. If it is still missing, check that the build output has no compilation errors and that the local stack is healthy. As a last resort, stop the worker, run docker compose restart in docker/, and start the worker again. Avoid docker compose down -v: it deletes the stack's data volumes.
documents.s: My node doesn't show up in the Workbench

documents.t: Look at the worker console (the bootRun output). Your execute() exception and stack trace are there. A node that fails and then runs again is being retried. If the cause can't change between attempts (bad settings, an unconnected port), throw NodeRuntimeException(isRetriable = false, …); see Errors, retries and progress. Reproduce it in a unit test with the same settings and input rows. This is faster than rerunning a workflow.
documents.s: My node appears but fails when it runs

documents.t: Symptom Cause and fix Plugin [id: 'org.projectcontinuum.worker', version: '…'] was not found continuumPlatformVersion in gradle.properties isn't a released version on Maven Central, or mavenCentral() is missing from pluginManagement.repositories in settings.gradle.kts. Unresolved reference 'databind' / 'ObjectMapper' Jackson 2 imports. Use tools.jackson.core.type.TypeReference and tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper, not com.fasterxml.jackson.*. validateContinuumNodeAnnotations FAILED A class extends ProcessNodeModel or TriggerNodeModel without @ContinuumNode. Unsupported class file major version or invalid source release: 21 The build runs on the wrong JDK. Run java -version and ./gradlew --version; both must report 21. Set JAVA_HOME to a JDK 21 and stop old daemons with ./gradlew --stop. Java heap space, GC overhead limit exceeded or the Gradle daemon dies during compilation Gradle needs more memory. The template sets org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx4g -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=1g in gradle.properties. Keep that line; if you removed it, put it back, and make sure the machine has the memory to spare. Port 8080 was already in use on bootRun The local API server uses 8080. Keep server.port: ${SERVER_PORT:8090} in application.yaml. Worker starts but logs connection errors for Kafka, Temporal or MinIO The local stack isn't running or isn't healthy. Run docker compose ps in docker/ and wait until every container is healthy. The stack needs about 8 GB of RAM, so raise Docker Desktop's memory limit if containers keep restarting or get killed. Worker starts but registers [] for both process and trigger nodes The worker didn't load your module. See the checklist above, steps 3 to 5. NoSuchBeanDefinitionException or UnsatisfiedDependencyException for your node at start-up The node's constructor asks for a bean Spring can't provide. Nodes can take ObjectMapper; anything else must be a bean from the worker. If in doubt, make the constructor empty. A node fails at random, or runs on the wrong worker Several workers share a task queue. Temporal gives work to whichever worker polls first, including one that doesn't have the node, and nothing warns you. Set a unique node-task-queue in application.yaml and taskQueue in the chart. IllegalArgumentException: Unsupported type while writing A cell value isn't a supported type (String, Int, Long, Float, Double, Boolean, List, Map or SVG). Convert it, or leave the key out instead of using null. See Reading and writing rows. CredentialsNotFoundException The credential name in the node's settings doesn't exist on the credentials server. In the local stack there is no credentials server at all; see Use a credential. Help page reads "Documentation not found" The .doc.md path doesn't match the node's full package and class name. For com.acme.demo.node.MyNodeModel it is src/main/resources/com/acme/demo/node/MyNodeModel.doc.md. See Step 4.

Symptom Cause and fix Helm: template: no template associated with name A rename in charts/ was only partly done. Every include "…" must match a define in _helpers.tpl. See Step 3. PR fails validate-versions Bump featureVersion in gradle.properties and set the chart's appVersion to the same value. See Step 6. Release workflow doesn't start on-release.yml and release.yml run on a published GitHub Release, not on a tag or a merge. See Step 6. Maven Central deploy fails with a namespace or signing error The group (your package) isn't a namespace you verified in the Central Portal, or the GPG secrets are missing. Verify the namespace, or switch publishing off; see Step 6. Jib push fails with 401 Unauthorized or denied DOCKER_HUB_USERNAME / DOCKER_HUB_PASSWORD are missing or wrong, or the account can't push to the repository named in jibToImage. See Step 6. Pod stuck in ImagePullBackOff The image name or tag in the chart doesn't exist, or the registry is private and the pod has no pull secret. See Step 6. Pod stuck in Init An init container is waiting for Kafka, Temporal or the API server. Its address in continuum.infra.* or continuum.apiServer doesn't match a real service. Check with kubectl get svc -n continuum and see Step 6. Pod fails to start because a Secret is missing continuum.secrets.existingMinioSecret names a Secret that doesn't exist in the namespace. See Step 6. Saved workflows break after a rename You renamed or moved a node class. The full class name is the node's identity in saved workflows, so don't rename classes after shipping.

continuum-feature-base ships 16 production-ready nodes for data transformation, filtering, aggregation, REST integration, scripting, and anomaly detection. 16 nodesKotlin / Spring BootData · Transform · Filter · REST · Scripting Category Node Description Data Create Table Creates a structured table from FreeMarker template configuration Data Column Join Joins two columns from left and right tables into one output column Data Joint Node Joins input strings into one Data Join on Multiple Keys Performs inner join on two tables using two key columns from each table Transform Pivot Columns Pivots table so pivot column values become new columns with value column as cell values Transform JSON Exploder Parses JSON strings and flattens keys into new columns Transform Column Splitter Splits a column into two parts Transform Kotlin Script Runs a Kotlin script for each row, adding a script_result column Filter Dynamic Row Filter Filters rows where the specified column value is greater than the threshold Filter Conditional Splitter Splits rows into two outputs based on threshold comparison Aggregation Time Window Aggregator Aggregates values into time windows, summing by window buckets Aggregation Batch Accumulator Groups rows into batches and adds batch_id and row_count columns Text Text Normalizer Normalizes text by trimming, lowercasing, and removing non-alphanumeric characters Security Crypto Hasher Generates SHA-256 hash of column values Analytics Anomaly Detector (Z-Score) Detects outliers using Z-score method (flags values with |Z| > 2) Integration REST Client Makes HTTP requests for each row using FreeMarker templated URLs and payloads See the continuum-feature-base README for build instructions and dependencies.

Built for computational chemistry, medicinal chemistry, and drug discovery teams who need scalable, reproducible molecular processing pipelines — parse, standardize, fingerprint, filter, react, and visualize molecules at scale. 38 nodes10 categoriesPowered by RDKit

Category Example nodes Calculators Calculate Charges, Descriptor Calculation (up to 41 descriptors) Converters Canonical SMILES, InChI ↔ Molecule, Molecule Writer, SMILES Parser Experimental Molecule Catalog Filter (PAINS/BRENK/NIH/ZINC), R-Group Decomposition, Structure Normalizer Fingerprints Fingerprint (9 algorithms), Count-Based Fingerprint, Fingerprint Similarity, Diversity Picker Fragments Molecule Fragmenter, Molecule Extractor, Murcko Scaffold Geometry Add Conformers, Add Coordinates, Optimize Geometry (MMFF94/UFF), Open 3D Alignment, RMSD Filter Modifiers Add/Remove Hydrogens, Aromatize, Kekulize, Salt Stripper Reactions Chemical Transformation, One/Two Component Reaction (SMARTS-based) Rendering RDKit to SVG Searching Substructure Filter/Counter, Functional Group Filter, Maximum Common Substructure Plus a Testing node (SDF Difference Checker) for validating molecular data pipelines.

Algorithm Type Typical use case Morgan (ECFP) Circular General-purpose similarity, QSAR, virtual screening FeatMorgan (FCFP) Circular (pharmacophoric) Pharmacophore-aware similarity AtomPair Topological Scaffold hopping, diversity analysis Torsion Topological Conformational similarity RDKit Path-based Substructure-oriented similarity Avalon Substructure Fast screening, patent searching Layered Path-based (layered) Similarity with tunable abstraction layers MACCS Structural keys (166-bit) Quick pharmacophore screening Pattern Substructure Substructure matching fingerprints

Physicochemical (AMW, SlogP, TPSA...), hydrogen bonding, structural counts, stereochemistry, ring systems, complexity, connectivity (Chi), and shape (Kier) descriptors — all computable in a single node pass.
The Molecule Catalog Filter node screens compounds against PAINS (assay interference), BRENK (unstable/reactive motifs), NIH (MLSMR exclusion filters), and ZINC (drug-likeness filters).

Project Continuum is an open-source, browser-native visual workflow platform — inspired by KNIME, built for the cloud. You design workflows as a drag-and-drop graph of nodes, and the platform runs them durably: a crashed worker, a dead Kafka broker, or a dropped connection doesn't lose your progress.
